item.title: Normalization by Evaluation with Substitutions as Operations
item.description: arXiv:2610.21131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In previous works on normalization by evaluation (NbE) with an untyped domain model, explicit substitutions are a major decision choice, which, in retrospect, is taken to simplify subsequent semantic proofs. This choice hence is taken for a purely technical reason. In addition, there is no obvious lemma to test the completeness of the definition or the laws for explicit substitutions. In this technical report, we investigate NbE in a typical setting, i.e. defining substitutions as operations. We show that this setting brings simplifications in proving syntactic properties and soundness of NbE, though complications are introduced in the completeness proof of NbE.
item.dc:creator: Jason Z. S. Hu

item.title: FAOPs: Normal Forms and an Algebra for AI Agent Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.22061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Organizations increasingly encode operational procedures as multi-step agent skills, here called Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), that must be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, requirements that regulated sectors make mandatory. Yet AOPs are typically kept as coarse-grained files, in which steps bundle actions, copied procedures drift apart, any step may reach any tool, and refactoring goes unchecked. We present Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that brings database-grade discipline to AI agent workflows. FAOP recasts each workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1) splits a workflow into atomic steps, Typed (FNF-2) makes its data flow explicit and type-checked, Factored (FNF-3) gives each shared procedure a single canonical definition so a change propagates instead of drifting, and Scoped (FNF-4) confines every step to least-privilege tool access. Once normalized, every atomic step is a separate entity with a declared contract and can be type-checked, scope-confined, bounded, tested, traced, and audited on its own. A FAOP algebra of provably sound equalities turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites; orthogonal extensions add verified termination (+V), optimization (+O), and time and cost bounds (+B); and an architectural-level classifier (0-3) determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. Together, these make integrity, isolation, typing, termination, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across the whole library, not runtime hopes. We implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system (what PostgreSQL is to data, SkillBase is to AOPs), together with a separate executor that enforces these guarantees at run time. A worked financial workflow illustrates the approach end to end.
item.dc:creator: Ali Mohammadi Shanghooshabad (JPMorgan Chase,Co.)

item.title: Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.22089v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum software relies on compilers, intermediate representations, and execution frameworks that transform programs before execution. Faults in these components can change the behavior of otherwise correct quantum programs. Yet quantum testing techniques are often evaluated using mutation-generated faults and curated bug benchmarks. We investigate how well the faults represented by these artifacts reflect those encountered in modern quantum software. We audit four quantum mutation-testing tools and three curated bug benchmarks, and collect 410 verified bugs from ten quantum software repositories over two years. We classify faults from all three sources into a common taxonomy of 56 bug families and compare their representation across mutation operators, curated benchmarks, and recent real-world bugs. The mutation tools support 20 bug families, and curated benchmarks add 15 more. Yet only 56 of the 410 real-world bugs (13.7%) belong to families represented by either source; the remaining 354 (86.3%) belong to families absent from both. The largest unrepresented families concern compiler transformations (66 bugs), type handling (53), and input validation (47). Unlike local gate or statement changes, these faults often depend on intermediate representations, compiler pipelines, input types, or dependency versions. Existing mutation operators primarily modify circuits and program constructs, whereas many real-world faults arise in the compilers, representations, and framework interfaces that process them. Addressing this gap requires looking beyond circuit-level faults toward testing semantic preservation across compiler transformations, correctness at representation boundaries, and interactions between software components. Our study provides empirical evidence to guide fault models and benchmarks that capture these mechanisms and preserve the contexts needed to reproduce them.
item.dc:creator: Asif Mohammed Saad, Ahsanul Ameen Sabit, Jonah Brandenburgh, Jiyuan Wang, Qian Zhang, Soneya Binta Hossain

item.title: A Gradual Probabilistic Lambda Calculus
item.description: arXiv:2604.05246v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probabilistic programming languages extend ordinary programming languages with the ability to sample values from probability distributions. Type systems can establish invariants of such programs, for instance by assigning to a program a distribution over types that specifies the probability of each kind of outcome. However, adopting such a type discipline can be cumbersome or overly conservative. Gradual typing addresses this problem by supporting a smooth transition between static and dynamic checking, and has been successfully applied for languages with different constructs and type abstractions. Nevertheless, its benefits have never been explored in the context of probabilistic languages. In this work, we present and formalize GLANG, a gradual source probabilistic lambda calculus. GLANG includes a binary probabilistic choice operator and allows programmers to gradually introduce/remove static type---and probability---annotations. The static semantics of GLANG heavily relies on the notion of probabilistic couplings, as required for defining several relations, such as consistency, precision, and consistent transitivity. The dynamic semantics of GLANG is given via elaboration to the target language TLANG, which features a distribution-based semantics interpreting programs as probability distributions over final values. Regarding the language metatheory, we establish that TLANG---and therefore also GLANG---is type safe and satisfies two of the so-called refined criteria for gradual languages, namely, that it is a conservative extension of a fully static variant and that it satisfies (a restricted form of) the gradual guarantee, behaving smoothly with respect to type precision. The metatheory is mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant.
item.dc:creator: Mat\'ias Toro, Federico Olmedo, Wenjia Ye

item.title: Language-Based Agent Control
item.description: arXiv:2605.12863v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control. In conventional programming, combinations of static typing and runtime enforcement have long been used to guarantee that well-typed programs satisfy user-specified policies, including policies for access control, information flow, data provenance, and more. The key idea behind LBAC is to extend these guarantees to agentic applications by requiring agents to generate programs that are themselves well typed in the context of the surrounding scaffolding code. Unsafe programs are rejected by the type-checker before execution, allowing policies to apply uniformly across the entire application, including both agent-generated behavior and developer-written scaffolding. At the same time, LBAC preserves substantial expressiveness: agents may perform arbitrary side-effect-free computation and recursively invoke subagents, which retain full tool access subject to the same -- or potentially more restrictive -- policies. We demonstrate LBAC with three case studies: I/O sandboxing via filesystem capabilities, data provenance, and information-flow control.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Zhou, Loris D'Antoni, Nadia Polikarpova

item.title: Fixed-Point Scaffolding in the Clef Programming Language
item.description: arXiv:2606.02854v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Native compilation changes how a program represents values and performs operations from processor to processor. In our view, proofs that justify source-level decisions must remain connected to those changes. We develop fixed-point scaffolding for this continuity in Clef and our Composer compiler. Our Program Semantic Graph retains types, joint constraints and proof dependencies. A thin MLIR middle end witnesses their settled consequences for native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA realization. The account connects nanopass traversal with preservation contracts, structural theorems and adjoint interfaces between reasoning modes. Four verification tiers organize automatic inference and reusable domain and system proofs, with probabilistic relations admitted at Tier 4. Established lower-tier facts can directly support richer derivations. We state conditions for composing lowering contracts and assembling compatible program segments, then show how their dependencies govern differential compilation after an edit. A worked foreign-call boundary follows source ranges through argument marshaling, the actual call and return conversion. Current FFI mechanisms bind checking evidence to those witnessed operations. A recent paper from Urschel provides elimination-growth bounds that supply a quantitative example. Reusable premises inform representation and error contracts that retain their sampling, arithmetic and exceptional-path assumptions. A further example admits value-indexed pairing through ordinary MLIR operations, connecting this scaffold to negative and fractional types. Together these constructions explain how a thin middle end can carry the consequences of rich source proofs into unboxed computation graphs. Integrity and efficiency share the same retained evidence. It justifies native realizations and identifies which analyses, proofs and lowered fragments remain reusable during development.
item.dc:creator: Houston Haynes

item.title: Negative and Fractional Types in the Fidelity Framework
item.description: arXiv:2606.04352v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Programs routinely create temporary data, retain state and revisit earlier results. Negative and fractional types benefit those activities in a type-resolved account of computation. Negative values redirect evaluation. Fractional values introduce value-specific auxiliary data and discharge it after a computation restores the required value. We develop both as first-class computational forms in our Clef design, using Chen and Sabry's directed, value-indexed calculus and distinguishing James and Sabry's logic-variable search interpretation. Our Program Semantic Graph retains their value identities and resource uses, enabling Composer to preserve their behavior through MLIR operations and native realization. In this paper, a negative-type counter and a fractional workspace calculation demonstrate the two constructions. Local proofs establish preservation of matching and independent resource discharge. Dimensional inference and proof terms supply premises through our four verification tiers. The applications connect deferred reverse computation to gradient calculations without an activation tape, and checked inverse steps to in-memory event recovery. A finite reconstruction horizon governs the exchange between storage and recomputation. We derive its error recurrence and show where Urschel's elimination-growth bounds can support a realized inverse step. Bayesian updates and quantum circuits supply further computational cases, including temporary workspace, measurement and a worked adiabatic schedule. Exact matching, bounded reconstruction and physical realization retain their respective contracts. The resulting architecture makes the information needed to run, reverse or complete a computation available to the compiler. Libraries can expose these operations through familiar interfaces while their retained structure supports unboxed execution and differential compilation across targets.
item.dc:creator: Houston Haynes

item.title: ANEForge: Python for direct computation on the Apple Neural Engine
item.description: arXiv:2606.17090v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ANEForge is a Python package that programs the Apple Neural Engine (ANE), the fixed-function neural accelerator on every recent Apple device, directly and without CoreML. In production the engine is reachable only through CoreML, which treats it as a scheduling option: no configuration requires the ANE, and a model can silently run on the CPU or GPU instead. ANEForge compiles a lazy tensor graph, built from 58 fused operators and 19 native bridge operators, into a single ANE program. The program is dispatched through the same ANE daemon and kernel-driver stack as Apple's internal framework. Beyond inference, the package reaches the engine's native fused attention, streams int8, int4, and sparse weights, keeps decoder and optimizer state resident across steps, and runs the forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer update of training on the engine. A small fused program completes a call in about 90us, near the engine's 70us per-program dispatch floor, and a pretrained ResNet-18 forward runs end-to-end in 0.33ms. ResNet-18, a sentence encoder, and a Vision Transformer run end-to-end against framework references, and a Stable Diffusion U-Net validates its forward pass. ANEForge targets Apple Silicon under macOS 14 and later. Each release is verified against a recorded macOS and ANE-compiler version.
item.dc:creator: Spencer H. Bryngelson

item.title: Bidirectional Elaborators \`a la Carte
item.description: arXiv:2607.09564v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Surface syntax in proof assistants like Rocq, Lean, Agda, and Idris is highly implicit, lacking many details that are needed for user-written code to denote precisely defined mathematical objects. Elaboration is an algorithm that accounts for these details by translating surface syntax to an explicit enough core syntax. The reliability and predictability of elaboration relies on several critical properties of the core type system, including decidability of judgemental equality and the injectivity of type constructors; these dependencies are witnessed in a concrete system by explicit calls to conversion checking and weak-head reduction subroutines. We introduce a dependently typed monadic domain specific language for the executable specification of correct-by-construction elaboration algorithms that is abstracted from any particular representation of normal forms or algorithm for conversion checking. In particular, we represent a bidirectionally typed surface language for Martin-L\"of type theory by shallow embedding in this DSL so that the translation of surface terms into core terms amounts to elementary equational calculation. This translation is correct by construction in the sense that it cannot produce ill-typed terms, and is automatically stable under judgemental equality of core terms and even under substitution; from the latter property, we obtain a new denotational interpretation of the suspension of elaboration problems. Finally, a concrete elaboration algorithm is extracted by algebraic means from a presheaf model of the DSL built out of the bi-initial natural model of Martin-L\"of type theory.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Slattery, Jonathan Sterling

item.title: Volition Elicitation: Operational Semantics for People and Their Machines
item.description: arXiv:2607.14138v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The most prevalent distributed systems today include people and their personal machines (smartphones), and computations in them are driven by people's volitions. Volition-guarded multiagent atomic transactions were proposed as an abstract specification language for such systems, in which a transaction has a precondition on the machine states of its participants and is guarded by the volitions of some of them. Here we develop an abstraction cascade that derives smartphone apps from such specifications and prove it correct down to the base programming language, GLP. The cascade consists of: (1) communicating volitional agents (CVA), which implement every local volition-guarded specification with simple guards, correctly, and completely for its strongly fair runs, by two-phase commit coordinated by the initiating agent; (2) volition-guarded GLP (vGLP), an extension of GLP with volitional procedures, whose goals put an interactively-typed question to the person, into which that implementation compiles; and (3) GLP, which implements vGLP by eliciting the person's answers through the widgets of their interactive types, correctly, and completely for complete widgets. We demonstrate the approach on three grassroots platforms --- a social graph, a social network, and currencies: a compiler carries the social graph and the currencies down the cascade to GLP programs that run with scripted persons, and earlier programs of the three run as mini-apps of one smartphone app.
item.dc:creator: Idit Keidar, Ehud Shapiro

item.title: Coexponential Exploration in the Clef Programming Language
item.description: arXiv:2610.12911v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clef was created as a concurrent programming language whose compiler tracks state ownership, waiting computations and request dependencies. We develop a coexponential account of stateful services and their client pools within this design. Delimited continuations retain the computation and resources needed to complete each interaction. These structures give our compiler premises for verifying service composition and preserving it through native lowering to multiple hardware targets. We connect finite actor state transitions to the initial, service and final rules of a coexponential server. A separate operational account relates actor dispatch to single-use continuation frames. We prove state-ownership and reply preservation, give a finite communication-summary analysis, and derive circular-wait exclusion under stated assumptions. A further result identifies when changing service order preserves both state and replies. Our Program Semantic Graph retains these facts through compilation. We are researching reusable proofs to confirm the ownership and communication interfaces, while our BAREWire implementation connects message meaning to its unboxed representation across respective endpoints. A distributed worker example preserves request identity across suspension, reordered replies and boundary conversion. Urschel's growth bounds inform a solver service; a distributed ADM update additionally preserves joint samples, metric evidence and request identity. Our two-category account connects component refinement, reusable proof terms and native realization. Protocols determine the admissible interactions, continuations expose their storage requirements, and retained dependencies support differential compilation. Developers can express ordinary stateful services while the compiler carries the conditions for their correct composition across execution targets.
item.dc:creator: Houston Haynes

item.title: Enhancing Knowledge Density via Hierarchical Context Pruning for Retrieval-Augmented Repository-Level Code Completion
item.description: arXiv:2508.10068v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has advanced repository-level code completion by retrieving external code snippets, API documentation, or type definitions to expand the model's contextual awareness. However, under the finite token budget of the context window, existing retrieval-augmented methods often saturate the budget with highly similar or even redundant code, which not only wastes tokens but also suppresses critical cross-file dependencies, preventing synergistic interaction between semantically similar reference snippets and cross-file dependency definitions. Therefore, further gains are limited by low knowledge density in the retrieved context rather than by model capacity. We propose SaraCoder, a retrieval-augmented framework that enhances knowledge density via hierarchical context pruning under a fixed context budget. A Hierarchical Feature Optimization module prunes an over-complete candidate pool in four stages. The freed tokens are then allocated to an External-Aware Identifier Disambiguator, which selectively injects only the most necessary cross-file dependency definitions. SaraCoder transforms context construction into a budget-aware optimization problem, balancing reference snippets and cross-file dependencies to build a context that is both knowledge-dense and semantically complete. Experiments on CrossCodeEval and RepoEval-Updated, across multiple backbone code LLMs, show that SaraCoder consistently outperforms strong RAG baselines such as GraphCoder and Repocoder in both code-level and identifier-level metrics, without increasing token usage, and yields synergistic gains when combined with other cross-file methods.
item.dc:creator: Xiaohan Chen, Xiang Chen, Yu Tian, Piji Li, Sheng-Jun Huang, Songcan Chen

item.title: LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language to Leverage Structure and Semantics at the LLM Interface
item.description: arXiv:2603.22519v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Textual Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a simple and familiar interface: a string of text is used for both input and output. However, the information conveyed to an LLM often has a richer structure and semantics, which is not conveyed in a string. For example, most prompts contain both instructions ("Summarize this paper into a paragraph") and data (the paper to summarize), but these are usually not distinguished when passed to the model. This can lead to model confusion and security risks, such as prompt injection attacks. This work addresses this shortcoming by introducing an LLM-native mark-up language, LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "Lemon"), that enables the structure and semantic metadata of the text to be communicated in a natural way to an LLM. This information can then be used during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation, leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security. This is analogous to how programming language types can be used for many purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting. We discuss the general design requirements of an LLM-native markup language, introduce the LLMON markup language and show how it meets these design requirements, describe how the information contained in a LLMON artifact can benefit model training and inference implementation, and provide some preliminary empirical evidence of its value for both of these use cases. We also discuss broader issues and research opportunities that are enabled with an LLM-native approach.
item.dc:creator: Michael Hind, Basel Shbita, Bo Wu, Farhan Ahmed, Chad DeLuca, Nathan Fulton, David Cox, Dan Gutfreund

item.title: SEVerA: Verified Synthesis of Self-Evolving Agents
item.description: arXiv:2603.25111v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances have shown the effectiveness of self-evolving LLM agents on tasks such as program repair and scientific discovery. In this paradigm, a planner LLM synthesizes an agent program that invokes parametric models, including LLMs, which are then tuned per task to improve performance. However, existing self-evolving agent frameworks provide no formal guarantees of safety or correctness. Because such programs are often executed autonomously on unseen inputs, this lack of guarantees raises reliability and security concerns. We formulate agentic code generation as a constrained learning problem, combining hard formal specifications with soft objectives capturing task utility. We introduce Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGM), which allow the planner LLM to specify a formal output contract for each generative model call using first-order logic. Each FGGM call wraps the underlying model in a rejection sampler with a verified fallback, ensuring every returned output satisfies the contract for any input and parameter setting. Building on FGGM, we present SEVerA (Self-Evolving Verified Agents), a three-stage framework: Search synthesizes candidate parametric programs containing FGGM calls; Verification proves correctness with respect to hard constraints for all parameter values, reducing the problem to unconstrained learning; and Learning applies scalable gradient-based optimization, including GRPO-style fine-tuning, to improve the soft objective while preserving correctness. We evaluate SEVerA on Dafny program verification, symbolic math synthesis, and policy-compliant agentic tool use ($\tau^2$-bench). Across tasks, SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations while improving performance over unconstrained and SOTA baselines, showing that formal behavioral constraints not only guarantee correctness but also steer synthesis toward higher-quality agents.
item.dc:creator: Debangshu Banerjee, Changming Xu, Eugene Ie, Ming Zhang, Daiyi Peng, Chu-Cheng Lin, Tarun Suresh, Gagandeep Singh

item.title: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
item.description: arXiv:2608.25061v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over the TorchPlan baseline at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup. Project page: https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench
item.dc:creator: Gokul Karthik Kumar, Yotam Perlitz, Corey Lammie, Andrea Giovannini, Katja Hose
